pages.title: Marvell raises fiscal 2031 revenue target at investor day
pages.text:
Marvell is targeting $70 billion to $90 billion in revenue by fiscal 2031
The chipmaker also raised its fiscal 2028 revenue goal to $20 billion, well above the analyst consensus of $18.2 billion
By Colleen Cabili·2 min read·Updated October 6, 2026
Marvell Technology held its investor day on Tuesday, setting a fiscal 2031 revenue target of $70 billion to $90 billion and lifting its fiscal 2028 goal to $20 billion. Marvell stock rose roughly 4% on the day.
The fiscal 2031 range marks Marvell's first-ever guidance for that year. The midpoint sits far above the analyst consensus of $47 billion, according to CNBC. The bottom of the range alone is more than 50% above the $45 billion that Piper Sandler had modeled for fiscal 2031, according to Benzinga. For context, Marvell posted $8.2 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.
The new fiscal 2028 target of $20 billion represents an increase from the $18 billion figure Marvell had provided when it reported second-quarter earnings in late August. Marvell attributed the additional $2 billion to demand for data center connectivity products, including interconnect scale-up optics and switching, the company said. Fiscal 2027 revenue is still expected at around $12 billion, the company said.
Marvell's business serving AI data centers breaks into two main areas. The company helps large cloud customers — including Amazon $AMZN and Alphabet $GOOGL — design and manufacture custom AI chips. It also makes the optical and networking chips that move data within and across data center racks. Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy said Marvell's AI addressable market could reach $400 billion by 2030, according to Benzinga.
Supporting the long-term outlook, Marvell forecast that capital expenditures for data centers would hit $3 trillion by 2030, compounding at roughly 35% annually between 2025 and 2030, the company said. Marvell noted that its projections account for spending growth slowing from its current pace as the forecast period progresses, the company said.
Marvell's custom chip business has a major customer in Google, with whom it expanded a commercial agreement in late July covering custom processors and related chips. Murphy indicated that the financial contribution from that agreement is not expected to materialize in a meaningful way until fiscal 2029 at the earliest, the company said.
Taken together, the successive upward revisions amount to a roughly 54% increase in the fiscal 2028 target over the span of about 10 months, according to Benzinga. Marvell stock has gained 217% over the past 12 months. Shares of data center connectivity peers Astera Labs and Credo Technology also rose Tuesday, gaining 8% and 6%, respectively, according to Benzinga.

pages.title: Marvell impresses Wall Street with strong earnings and a much bigger long-term outlook
pages.text:
Marvell impresses Wall Street with strong earnings and a much bigger long-term outlook
The chipmaker raised its fiscal 2031 revenue target to between $70 billion and $90 billion, and its stock jumped nearly 8% intraday
Marvell Technology gave Wall Street a growth story it could not ignore. At its Investor Day on October 6, 2026, CEO Matt Murphy laid out a fiscal 2031 revenue target of between $70 billion and $90 billion.
For context, the company’s expected fiscal 2026 revenue is $8.2 billion. Murphy is pitching a business roughly an order of magnitude larger within about five fiscal years, and investors seemed willing to hear him out.
Shares of Marvell (MRVL) climbed nearly 8% intraday after the presentation.
The long-range target did not arrive in a vacuum. It followed Marvell’s fiscal Q2 2027 report, which showed record quarterly revenue of $2.74 billion.
That figure was up 37% year-over-year.
The real engine was the data center. That segment brought in $2.17 billion in the quarter, a 46% increase from a year earlier.
Data-center sales made up 79% of total revenue.
Management also lifted its full-year view. Marvell now sees fiscal 2027 revenue of approximately $12 billion, which would represent about 45% growth year over year.

We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
Within that, the company anticipates data-center growth of nearly 60%.
The medium-term target moved too. Marvell revised its fiscal 2028 revenue guidance up to approximately $20 billion, from a prior estimate of around $18 billion.
The company identified three main growth drivers: AI connectivity, custom silicon and optical solutions.
AI connectivity refers to the hardware that links thousands of processors so they can work as one giant computer. Training large AI models requires constant, high-speed communication between chips, and bottlenecks there can waste expensive compute.
Custom silicon means designing chips tailored to a specific customer’s workloads. Large cloud operators increasingly want processors built for their own needs instead of buying only off-the-shelf parts, and Marvell helps design and build them.
Optical solutions use light instead of electrical signals to move data. Over longer distances and at higher speeds, optics can carry more information with less power, which matters when data centers are scaling up rapidly.
A $70 billion to $90 billion fiscal 2031 range is notably wide. The $20 billion spread between the low and high ends is larger than the company’s entire fiscal 2028 target.
What this means for investors and the AI trade
With data centers making up 79% of revenue, the stock’s fortunes are now tightly linked to AI capital spending.
The most useful checkpoints will be the next few quarterly reports. Investors will want to see whether Marvell stays on track for approximately $12 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue and nearly 60% data-center growth.
Progress toward the roughly $20 billion fiscal 2028 target will be the next real test.

pages.title: Analysts set Marvell (MRVL) share price target for 12 months
pages.text:
Even though Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL) stock has corrected nearly 5% over the past five days through September 29, 2026, several Wall Street analysts have reaffirmed their bullish outlook for this company.
Over the past three days, four analysts have signaled further upside for the MRVL share price for the next 12 months. On September 27, Srini Pajjuri, an expert at RBC Capital, reiterated a ‘Buy’ rating for Marvell stock.
Pajjuri maintained the firm’s 12-month price target for MRVL share price at $360, thereby indicating a potential 42.91% upside. On Monday, Timothy Arcuri, an analyst at UBS, issued a ‘Buy’ rating for Marvell and raised the 12-month price target to $335 from $310.
On September 28, C J Muse, a researcher at Cantor Fitzgerald, reiterated a ‘Hold’ rating for MRVL. Muse, however, lifted the firm’s 12-month price target to $330 from $300.
This analyst based his bullish thesis on the substantial long-term artificial intelligence (AI) growth drivers and a unique revenue acceleration trajectory.
On Tuesday, Atif Malik, an expert at Citigroup Inc. (NYSE: C), maintained a ‘Buy’ rating for the MRVL share price. He set the bank’s 12-month price target for Marvell stock at $275, suggesting around a 9% gain.
Following these bullish ratings for Marvell stock, 28 Wall Street analysts surveyed by TipRanks over the last 3 months have set an average price target of $299.29.
MRVL share price predictions. Source: TipRanks
The highest and the lowest MRVL forecasts from these sampled analysts are $400 and $220, respectively.
Is Marvell a good stock to buy?
Over the last 12 months, Marvell’s stock has rallied by over 205%, driven by the AI boom. As such, the company’s market capitalization has soared to $226.4 billion at the time of reporting.
With MRVL’s share price having jumped by more than 135% over the past 6 months, Wall Street analysts expect more upside over the next 12 months.

Marvell rides the AI boom, targets $90B in revenue by fiscal 2031
Marvell Technology (MRVL) stock is getting a boost after outlining a new growth target at the company's investor day, namely $90 billion in revenue by its fiscal year 2031.
Yahoo Finance Tech Editor Dan Howley breaks down the news out of Marvell's investor day.
Dan, break this all down for us.
Yeah, bro, this is as you said, part of their investor day and the the big kind of to-do here comes down to their custom chip offerings. They build custom chips for the likes of Google and Amazon. They have a huge deal with Google, uh, that is a multi-year long agreement, north of $100 billion, uh, if they complete all of, uh, the different steps involved and it hits certain milestones. Now, the reason why the the stock is up today is likely because of the revised estimates that they have for forward-looking guidance. Now, for 2028, uh they say that they are expecting upwards of $20 billion in revenue. That's higher than what the street was originally expecting and it's worth pointing out, this is not two years away. This is less than a year away. They're currently in their fiscal 2027, uh, Q3. So not too far off for them for their fiscal 2028. Uh, and then they're also looking at the 2030 revenue guidance. They put that between 70 to $90 billion. Uh, that's far more than the uh original Wall Street estimates. So, obviously, they see a lot of advancements here from their custom chip business and what that means for the company going forward as we continue to see more companies like Google, like Amazon, look for ways to wean themselves off of Nvidia's uh the the dependence on Nvidia, as well as begin to rent out those chips to third parties. Don't forget, Amazon, it says that its chip business could be a $50 billion uh a year business if it didn't have to gobble up most of its chips for its own processing. and Google also is looking to rent out its own chips as well. So, this could be huge for Marvell if they're able to continue to provide the necessary components and Google and Amazon can get additional customers.
Dan, you can't help but notice Marvell stock up 240% year to date. I'm taking a look at Alpha space right now and that is such momentum and up today just about 7%. So definitely one to watch. Dan Howley, thanks so much for bringing that all down. Appreciate it.

A 9.5% intraday pop at $296.69 adds roughly $23 billion of market value to a $260 billion chipmaker in a single session. Moves this size are rare here, so keep an eye on whether it holds into the close.
Marvell Technology climbed to $296.69 by early afternoon, adding roughly $23 billion of market value in a single session. For a chip stock of this size, a near 10% one-day swing is uncommon.
Intraday moves this large in mega-cap semiconductors signal a shift in how the market prices the stock, whether sentiment around AI-driven chip demand, institutional repositioning, or sector rotation. The size of the gain makes it worth watching closely.
The key question for investors now is whether the stock holds these levels into the close. A close near $296.69 confirms that buyers committed at elevated prices.
Regular trading hours moves of this magnitude in a stock with Marvell's market footprint set the tone for the days that follow, as other market participants reassess their positions. “AI-related bookings remain exceptionally robust, and we expect our revenue growth to accelerate further through the remainder of fiscal 2027. Given this strength, we are again raising our revenue outlook for both fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 compared with the guidance we provided last quarter.
Second straight quarter Marvell has lifted its revenue outlook, and this time the raise covers both fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 on custom AI silicon bookings. Guidance that far out moving twice in a row is the signal to track here.

Data center growth is accelerating: Murphy's segment is now outrunning the company's overall pace, evidence AI infrastructure budgets are spreading past the biggest chipmakers. For a $211.7 billion company still treated as a second-tier custom silicon play, that gap matters.

Murphy just put a date on the custom silicon ramp: the second half of fiscal 2027, with the full roadmap due at the October 6 Investor Day. For a $211.7 billion chipmaker whose bull case rests on winning custom AI accelerator sockets, that timeline is the thing to hold management to.

pages.title: Marvell Now Sees as Much as $90 Billion in Annual Sales by Fiscal 2031. Here's Why It's a Chip Stock to Buy. | The Motley Fool
pages.text:
▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool
Marvell Technology (MRVL +5.81%) finally put a number on its long-term goals. Talking to investors in New York on Tuesday, management said Marvell sees revenue of around $20 billion in fiscal 2028 and $70 billion to $90 billion in fiscal 2031 (the year ending in early 2031).
For context, Marvell took in $8.2 billion of revenue in fiscal 2026, the year that ended in January. So the latest range is about 8.5 to 11 times last fiscal year's sales. Management also pegged the size of the market it's chasing at about $400 billion by 2030.
Shares jumped after the event and were around $290 as of this writing. At that price, the stock trades at about 43 times the earnings expected for fiscal 2028, so it's not cheap on near-term numbers.
Compared with the company's own long-term targets, though, I think the price looks much more reasonable.
Image source: Getty Images.
Marvell's fiscal 2028 revenue forecast has risen in each of its past two updates. In May, management called for around $16.5 billion. In August, it upped that to around $18 billion, on top of about $12 billion expected for fiscal 2027. Now it sees about $20 billion, an 11% gain over about six weeks.
The growth Marvell expects for that year has climbed with it, from around 45% in May to about 50% in August. If fiscal 2027 lands near that $12 billion forecast, $20 billion would mean growth of about 67%. In other words, Marvell keeps finding more growth for the same year, even as the company gets bigger.
Reported results are going the same way. Revenue rose 37% year over year in the fiscal second quarter (the period ended Aug. 1), up from 28% the quarter before, and the company forecast more than 50% growth this quarter.
The fiscal 2031 range calls for more of the same. Going from $20 billion to $70 billion to $90 billion in three years would take annual growth of around 52% to 65% -- about the rate Marvell now expects for fiscal 2028, held for another three years.
Today's price looks modest against the targets
On the August earnings call, Dan Durn, Marvell's chief financial officer, said its non-GAAP (adjusted) operating margin would probably hit the company's 38% to 40% long-term target range by the fiscal fourth quarter and reach the top end in fiscal 2028. He added Marvell would reset that long-term model at the investor day. The adjusted operating margin was 36.6% last quarter, up from 34.8% a year before.
Even at the old 38% to 40% range, $70 billion to $90 billion of revenue would mean around $27 billion to $36 billion of adjusted operating profit in fiscal 2031. Marvell's market value, meanwhile, is about $255 billion. So the stock sells for around 7 to 10 times the fiscal 2031 operating profit implied by its own targets.
Operating profit isn't earnings, of course. But with Marvell expecting an adjusted tax rate of only about 13% in fiscal 2028, taxes might not change the picture much.
If Marvell hit only half the low end of its range, or $35 billion, a 38% margin would mean shares cost about 19 times operating profit. For a company growing so fast, I'd call that a fair price for a disappointing outcome.
How solid is the range?
Of course, a target isn't a contract. And the $20 billion gap between the low and high ends of the fiscal 2031 range matches Marvell's entire fiscal 2028 target.
I couldn't find any disclosed customer commitments backing the range. CEO Matt Murphy said custom chip programs with cloud giants such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon could lift revenue as they grow after 2029.
Even the custom deal Marvell has detailed most fully leaves the buying up to the customer. A warrant Marvell issued in August to Google, a unit of Alphabet, vests as Google buys custom products, up to $120 billion worth through fiscal 2033. But the filing describing it calls the purchases "discretionary."
$252BMarket cap calculated using publicly traded shares outstanding only. Does not include unlisted, private, or dual-class non-traded shares. Implied market cap may vary.
Growth in custom chips also drags on profitability. Management said the custom ramp is why its adjusted gross margin guidance for the fiscal third quarter is 57.5% to 58.5%, below 58.9% last quarter.
And spending on artificial intelligence could slow long before 2031.
Still, I don't think Marvell needs to hit its range for the stock to do well from here. At about $290, shares look fairly priced even against half the low end, and the shorter-term outlook keeps rising. I think the stock is worth buying today, even after Tuesday's jump. But I'd expect big swings in the share price ahead.

pages.title: Marvell Analysts Chase the AI Vision Higher as Targets Jump to $450
pages.text:
Sie befinden sich hier: Startseite > Börse > Unternehmensnachrichten > Marvell Analysts Chase the AI Vision Higher as Targets ...
Architektur-Render eines gläsernen Firmensitzes repräsentiert Marvell Technology, Aktie ISIN US5738741041, moderne Halbleiterbranche Illustration mit AI erstellt.
Two of Wall Street's better-known research shops moved in tandem on Tuesday, lifting their price objectives on Marvell Technology after the chipmaker sketched out a far more ambitious revenue map at its investor day. Jefferies raised its target to $450 from $325 while keeping a Buy rating, and Evercore ISI lifted its own to $433 from $275 with an Outperform stance intact.
The stock caught a modest bid in premarket trading, adding 0.7% to change hands at EUR 256.85. That follows a 5.6% surge in the prior session that carried the shares to a close of EUR 255.15, a move attributed chiefly to the upgraded long-range forecasts and helped along by a broadly firmer technology tape.
A Bigger Pie by 2028 — and a Far Bigger One by 2031
At the center of the analysts' enthusiasm sits Marvell's revised outlook. Management now targets roughly $20 billion in revenue for fiscal 2028, up from the $18 billion goal it had set out only in August. The company also raised its revenue objective for custom solutions in fiscal 2029 to more than $12 billion.
The horizon stretches much further, though. For fiscal 2031, Marvell laid out a revenue range of $70 billion to $90 billion alongside adjusted earnings per share — non-GAAP — of $30 or more. Management anchored those figures to the breakneck expansion of the artificial intelligence market, which Marvell sizes at roughly $400 billion in total addressable demand for AI applications by 2030.
Jefferies leaned explicitly on that fiscal 2031 framework, pointing to the connectivity segment's potential as the justification for its richer valuation. Evercore's revision followed the same logic, with both houses rewarding the company's long-term positioning rather than near-term results.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Marvell Technology?
Substrates, a Dividend, and a Routine Insider Sale
Capacity is the quiet prerequisite for all of that growth, and Marvell is moving to secure it. AT&S announced on September 22 an expanded collaboration with the chipmaker aimed at scaling output of advanced IC substrates — the building blocks required for next-generation AI and cloud infrastructure.
On the capital-returns side, the board declared a regular quarterly dividend of $0.06 per share on September 25. Shareholders of record as of October 9, 2026 will receive the payout on October 29, 2026.
A filing also disclosed that a family trust tied to President and COO Chris Koopmans sold 10,000 shares on October 1 under a pre-arranged Rule 10b5-1 trading plan. The manager retains indirect ownership of 207,941 shares following the transaction.
The rally has narrowed the gap to the 52-week high of EUR 290.35, leaving the stock about 12% below that peak. Since the start of the year, the shares have climbed 250%.
That kind of run leaves little room for error. Celebrating targets set years into the future effectively prices in a largely frictionless execution, and any unexpected slowdown in hyperscaler infrastructure budgets would land hard on a valuation this rich. The distance to those out-year goals is considerable, and a business that must multiply several times over by the start of the next decade offers no cushion for operational disappointment.
Even so, the strategic case remains intact. Marvell's grip on custom silicon for data centers has become central to the AI supply chain, and the steady dividend alongside heavy investment in future chip generations signals both discipline and confidence. For now, the balance of opportunity still tilts toward the specialized data-center chip story — provided the company delivers on the very promises that sent its shares flying.

Marvell Is The Latest AI Infra Play To Raise Long-Term Targets: Here's How Dell, HPE, CoreWeave And Broadcom Compare
Companies across chips, networking, servers and data centers are gaining greater revenue visibility amid the AI infrastructure boom.
Construction workers wire electricity lines in a data center in Dallas, Texas on March 4, 2026. (Tom Fox/The Dallas Morning News via Getty Images)
Marvell sees custom AI chips becoming a roughly $30 billion business by fiscal 2031.
Dell, HPE, CoreWeave and Broadcom raised revenue expectations in their recent quarterly reports.
Hyperscaler spending could approach $800 billion this year, creating a broad tailwind for the AI infrastructure ecosystem.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Marvell Technology, Inc.’s (MRVL) stock posted its best session in over a month on Tuesday after the chipmaker set long-term revenue targets at its investor day, joining several artificial intelligence infrastructure companies that have raised forecasts in recent months.
But a closer look at the second-quarter results shows the signals were already on the wall.
Several key AI infrastructure companies, including CoreWeave (CRWV), Dell Technologies (DELL), Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), and Broadcom (AVGO), have also raised their revenue expectations in recent months, indicating that the AI infrastructure buildout is far from over.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
The common thread is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Companies across the infrastructure stack are starting to see stronger demand translate into more visibility for revenue several years out.
From custom AI chips and networking equipment to AI-optimized servers and the data centers needed to house them, the spending cycle is broadening across the ecosystem.
MRVL stock jumped nearly 6% Tuesday following its outlook at its Investor Day event, although shares fell slightly in premarket trading Wednesday.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Marvell laid out a fiscal 2031 revenue target of $70 billion-$90 billion, implying a massive expansion from the $8.2 billion it generated in fiscal 2026, which ended in January 2026.
Marvell expects its custom-made AI chips business to generate about $30 billion in revenue by fiscal 2031. Beyond that, the company sees more opportunities in other data-center components, including networking chips and technology that helps AI systems process data faster.
The company also raised its fiscal 2028 revenue target to approximately $20 billion, from $18 billion previously, and expects more than $12 billion of custom revenue in fiscal 2029.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Importantly, this was not a sudden change in tone. In Q2, Marvell reported record revenue of $2.74 billion, up 37% year over year, while data-center revenue surged 46%. CEO Matt Murphy said at the time that AI-related bookings remained “exceptionally robust” and that growth should accelerate through the rest of fiscal 2027.
Analysts React To Marvell’s Lofty Outlook
Jefferies raised its price target on MRVL to $450 from $325, saying Marvell’s FY31 outlook puts “connectivity at the center of the story,” with interconnect potentially reaching $37.5 billion and custom revenue approaching $30 billion.
Evercore ISI lifted its target to $433 from $275, highlighting Marvell’s IP portfolio and flexible business model across merchant, semi-custom and custom solutions.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
Marvell is becoming more than a custom-chip play as networking and connectivity gain importance in AI infrastructure, the research firm said in its note to investors.
Raymond James similarly called the FY31 outlook “extraordinary,” saying scale-up connectivity and optics could prove “at least as important” to the long-term story as custom compute.
Morningstar raised its fair value estimate to $360 from $300, citing a roughly 40% increase in its fiscal 2031 revenue and EPS estimates. It acknowledged valuation concerns after the stock’s sharp run-up, but said the company’s expected growth makes the premium easier to justify.
Advertisement|Remove ads.
On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for MRVL flipped to ‘bullish’ from ‘bearish’ on Wednesday. MRVL shares have already gained 238% so far this year.
The AI Infrastructure Signal Is Getting Louder
Marvell is hardly alone. CoreWeave raised its FY2026 revenue outlook to $12.4 billion-$13.2 billion, while HPE lifted FY2026 revenue growth to 34%-37% and its FY2027 guidance to 13%-17%. Dell raised FY2027 revenue guidance by $25 billion to $192 billion
Broadcom, meanwhile, now expects AI semiconductor revenue of roughly $115 billion in fiscal 2027, up from its previous expectation of more than $100 billion.

Even Synopsys has raised its FY2026 revenue outlook, citing continued AI-driven demand for silicon IP and engineering solutions.

Taken together, these upgrades suggest the AI trade is increasingly moving beyond near-term enthusiasm.
Microsoft (MSFT), Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Meta Platforms (META) continue to ramp up capital spending to build the computing capacity needed for AI. As such, the hyperscaler capital spending is expected to approach $800 billion in 2026 and could top $1 trillion in 2027, creating a powerful multiplier effect for semiconductor and networking companies.

Marvell Technology (MRVL) Stock: Gains as AI Chip Demand Fuels Bullish Forecast
Marvell raises its FY2028 revenue target as custom silicon and data center demand strengthen growth
By Yasmin WernerOctober 6, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Marvell stock gains as FY2028 revenue guidance rises to $20 billion
The company expects fiscal 2028 revenue growth of about 67% year over year
AI chip and data center demand remain central to Marvell’s growth outlook
Amazon, Google, and Microsoft support Marvell’s custom silicon expansion
Marvell shares have climbed more than 240% since the start of the year
Marvell Technology (MRVL) stock gained 5.64% to $286.58 during Tuesday trading after the company raised its long-term revenue guidance. The semiconductor company now expects fiscal 2028 revenue to reach about $20 billion. The stronger forecast reflects expanding demand for custom chips and data center infrastructure.
The updated outlook marks a significant increase from Marvell’s previous fiscal 2028 revenue target. Management had projected about $18 billion in August, while market estimates had centered near $18.2 billion. Therefore, the latest guidance places Marvell above its earlier expectations for the period.
Marvell also expects fiscal 2028 revenue to rise about 67% from the previous year. Chief Executive Matt Murphy presented the updated targets during the company’s investor day conference Tuesday. The announcement strengthened attention around Marvell’s growing exposure to large-scale computing infrastructure.
Marvell Raises Fiscal 2028 Revenue Target
Marvell expects demand from large technology companies to support its revenue expansion through fiscal 2028. The company develops custom silicon and networking products for high-performance computing systems. These products help data centers move information efficiently between processors, memory, and other infrastructure components.
The company estimates its total addressable market related to artificial intelligence could reach approximately $400 billion by 2030. Marvell works on custom silicon programs with major technology companies, including Amazon, Google, and Microsoft. Consequently, these partnerships give Marvell exposure to continued spending on large data center projects.
Marvell competes directly with Broadcom across several semiconductor infrastructure markets. Both companies provide networking technologies and custom processors used in advanced computing systems. However, Marvell has expanded its position through custom chip programs and high-speed connectivity products.
Semiconductor Demand Supports Marvell Growth
Semiconductor companies have benefited from rising spending on computing capacity and large data centers this year. Marvell has participated in that expansion through products designed for networking and custom processing workloads. Meanwhile, technology companies continue building infrastructure that requires faster data transfer and greater computing efficiency.
Marvell also gained broader market exposure after joining the S&P 500 index in June. The inclusion followed substantial share appreciation during 2026 and increased the company’s presence within major equity benchmarks. Marvell shares have climbed more than 240% since the beginning of the year.
Earlier this year, Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang highlighted Marvell’s position within the semiconductor industry. The company has since continued expanding its custom silicon and networking businesses. Its latest fiscal 2028 forecast now reinforces management’s expectations for substantial revenue growth.
Marvell Expands Role in Data Center Infrastructure
Marvell designs high-speed infrastructure that connects processors across modern data centers. Its portfolio includes networking, connectivity, storage, and custom semiconductor products. These technologies support cloud computing providers that require large amounts of processing capacity.
The company has increasingly focused on custom silicon programs for major hyperscale customers. Those projects allow large technology companies to develop specialized chips for specific computing workloads. Marvell provides design expertise and semiconductor technologies that support those customized platforms.
The revised revenue outlook adds another growth target to Marvell’s expanding data center business. Management now expects stronger fiscal 2028 sales than projected only two months earlier. The increase reflects the company’s larger role in custom silicon and high-speed data center infrastructure.

rallied on advanced optical interconnect demonstrations for AI data centers.
Custom silicon relationships with major operators anchor the company's growth story.
A neutral, platform-agnostic stance positions it across the AI infrastructure buildout.
Marvell Technology Group Ltd (NASDAQ:MRVL)
rallied this week after unveiling advanced optical interconnect technology aimed at the connectivity bottlenecks inside artificial intelligence data centers, reinforcing its role in the buildout of large computing clusters. The chipmaker showcased next-generation optical demonstrations at a major industry conference, and the reception lifted the stock during recent sessions. With custom silicon and high-speed connectivity anchoring its story, Marvell Technology
Marvell Technology Group Ltd (NASDAQ:MRVL)
featured prominently in coverage of the infrastructure powering advanced models.
The company drew attention after demonstrating advanced optical interconnect technology designed to move data faster between the components of artificial intelligence systems. The showcase, tied to a leading optical communications conference, highlighted Marvell Technology's push into the plumbing that links accelerators, switches, and memory across sprawling data centers. Shares advanced as the market digested the announcement, placing the name among the more active constituents of the Nasdaq Composite during a strong stretch for infrastructure chips.
The showcase resonated because connectivity has emerged as one of the defining challenges of large-scale computing. As clusters grow, the difficulty of moving data quickly between components has become a genuine constraint on performance. Marvell Technology's demonstrations spoke directly to this pain point, offering technology aimed at relieving the bottleneck. The market's swift reaction reflected recognition that advances in connectivity can unlock the full value of the accelerators operators have been racing to deploy across their facilities.
Marvell Technology designs semiconductors that move and manage data across networks and inside data centers. Its portfolio spans custom silicon built for specific customers, high-speed connectivity chips, optical technology, and networking components. The firm has carved out a role as a supplier of the specialized parts that stitch together large computing systems. As artificial intelligence workloads have grown, the demand for faster, more efficient data movement has placed Marvell Technology's products at the center of the infrastructure conversation.
The company's breadth across custom silicon, connectivity, and optical technology gives it multiple points of contact with the systems powering advanced computing. Rather than betting on a single product line, it supplies a range of components that operators need to assemble and scale their clusters. This diversity lets the firm participate in the buildout from several angles, cushioning it against shifts in any one segment. Its role as a supplier of the connective and custom elements of large systems has grown steadily more central.
The bottleneck in modern computing clusters increasingly lies not in raw processing but in moving data between components fast enough to keep accelerators fed. Marvell Technology's optical interconnect demonstrations addressed exactly this challenge, showcasing technology that pushes more data through each connection. Advanced optical modules and co-packaged optics aim to scale the connectivity of large systems, allowing operators to link more accelerators without choking on data transfer limits. This focus on the connective tissue of data centers has become a defining part of the company's story.
Co-packaged optics and advanced optical modules represent a frontier in how data centers scale, capable of moving far more information through each connection while managing power. As clusters expand, the limits of conventional connectivity become more apparent, elevating the value of optical approaches. Marvell Technology's demonstrations positioned it at this frontier, showcasing technology designed to keep pace with the escalating demands of advanced computing. This focus on the connective tissue of systems has become a signature element of its story.
A cornerstone of Marvell Technology's positioning is its custom silicon work, designing chips tailored to the needs of specific large customers. The company has described relationships spanning the major operators of hyperscale computing, building bespoke accelerators and networking parts to their specifications. This business ties the firm directly to the spending plans of the largest builders of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Custom silicon has emerged as a powerful growth engine, since each design win can translate into sustained demand as customers scale their systems.
Design wins in custom silicon can prove especially durable, since customers that commit to a bespoke chip tend to build entire systems around it. This stickiness translates into sustained demand as those systems scale, giving the company visibility into coming periods. Marvell Technology has emphasized its relationships with major operators as a foundation for this business. The bespoke nature of the work deepens ties with customers, embedding the firm in the plans of the largest builders of advanced computing infrastructure.
Marvell Technology has described itself as a neutral supplier working across the industry rather than favoring any single platform. This positioning lets it serve many customers, providing the connectivity and custom silicon that different systems require regardless of which accelerators sit at their core.
Marvell Technology's trajectory intertwines with the wider semiconductor surge tied to artificial intelligence. As accelerator makers push new platforms, the demand for supporting connectivity and custom silicon rises in tandem. The company sits alongside the AI Stocks drawing intense attention as the buildout accelerates, its products serving as essential complements to the accelerators that grab headlines. This link places Marvell Technology firmly within the group of firms whose fortunes track the health of the broader infrastructure theme.
Entering the final days of September, Marvell Technology
Marvell Technology Group Ltd (NASDAQ:MRVL)
stands out as a supplier of the connectivity and custom silicon that bind large computing clusters together. With advanced optical technology, deep customer relationships, and a neutral stance across platforms, the company remains firmly among the names tied to the infrastructure powering the artificial intelligence buildout.

It designs semiconductors for data movement and networking, including custom silicon, high-speed connectivity, and optical technology for data centers.
Why did Marvell Technology rally?
It unveiled advanced optical interconnect technology aimed at connectivity bottlenecks inside AI data centers.
What is Marvell's custom silicon business?
It designs bespoke chips tailored to specific large customers, tying the firm to the spending plans of major infrastructure builders.

pages.title: Evercore ISI raises Marvell price target to $433 after Investor Day
pages.text:
Evercore ISI raises Marvell price target to $433 after Investor Day
The firm kept its Outperform rating after Marvell lifted its long-term revenue guidance on surging AI data center demand
Evercore ISI has raised its price target on Marvell Technology (MRVL) to $433, up from $155, and kept its Outperform rating on the stock.
That something was Marvell’s Investor Day on October 6, 2026. Management used the event to rewrite its long-term revenue outlook, and the new numbers were large enough to send analysts back to their spreadsheets.
The headline revision came in fiscal 2028. Marvell now expects revenue of approximately $20 billion that year, up from a previous target of $18 billion. That figure also came in ahead of broader market estimates.
Then came the bigger swing. Marvell set a fiscal 2031 revenue goal of $70 billion to $90 billion.
The driver, according to Marvell, is AI data center demand. The company pegs its AI total addressable market at approximately $400 billion by 2030.
Marvell also pointed to momentum it can already show. Its data center revenue reportedly grew about 46% year-over-year in one of its recent quarters.
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
Investors liked what they heard. Marvell shares jumped roughly 7% to 10% intraday after the announcements.
Evercore ISI was not alone in raising the bar. HSBC lifted its price target on Marvell to $450 on October 2, 2026, a few days before the Investor Day event. That timing is worth noting. HSBC placed its bet ahead of the guidance update, while Evercore waited for management’s numbers and then made a much larger jump from its prior target.
Morgan Stanley has also adjusted its price target on the stock.
But the risks deserve equal billing. The fiscal 2031 range is wide, with a $20 billion gap between the low and high ends.
Those targets also depend heavily on one theme. If AI infrastructure spending slows, gets delayed or shifts toward competitors, the path from roughly $20 billion to $70 billion or more gets much steeper.
What to watch next is execution. The fiscal 2028 target of approximately $20 billion is the nearer milestone and the more testable one.
Investors should also keep an eye on whether data center growth holds near the reported 46% pace. That metric is the clearest real-time read on whether the AI demand Marvell is describing continues to materialize.

pages.title: Wall Street analyst sets Marvell (MRVL) stock price target for 12 months
pages.text:
As Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL) stock fell by more than 5% over the past 30 days through September 18, 2026, Joseph Moore, a Wall Street analyst at Morgan Stanley (NYSE: MS), expects less upside over the next 12 months.
Moore maintained a ‘Hold’ rating for MRVL stock, according to a note sent to clients on Friday. He also reaffirmed the bank’s 12-month price target for Marvell stock at $246, thereby signaling a potential upside of 3.96%.
Morgan Stanley based its ‘Hold’ rating on the fact that the MRVL stock traded at more than twice the valuation multiple of peer leaders, including Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO) and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ: NVDA). As such, this analyst argued that the company’s elevated valuation leaves insufficient room for further expansion over the next 12 months.
He highlighted that although Marvell has accelerated its data center growth outlook to approximately 60% for calendar year 2027 and continues to expand its position in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure through XPU attach, optical connectivity, and scale-up networking, these positive developments are already fully reflected in elevated market expectations.
Is Marvell a good stock to buy?
At the time of writing, 27 Wall Street analysts surveyed by TipRanks over the last three months have set an average rating of ‘Strong Buy’ for Marvell stock
These analysts have set an average price target for MRVL at $398.38. The highest price target for MRVL from these experts is $400, while the lowest is $220.
Over the past 12 months, MRVL stock has rallied more than 218%, trading at $236.62 at the time of publication. As a result, this company has a market capitalization of approximately $216.4 billion.

Marvell Technology (MRVL) Stock Trades Up, Here Is Why
Tue, October 6, 2026 at 2:52 PM PDT 2 min read
What Happened?
Shares of networking chips designer Marvell Technology (NASDAQ: MRVL) jumped 8% in the morning session after the company raised its 2028 revenue forecast to approximately $20 billion from an earlier projection of $18 billion, citing strong demand for chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers as reported by Reuters.
The updated forecast represents an increase of approximately $2 billion over the previous $18 billion projection for 2028. Marvell attributed the higher target to strong demand for chips used in data centers, including artificial intelligence applications. The revision reflects the company's increased revenue expectations for its data center chip business.
After the initial pop, the shares cooled down to $280.82, up 3.6% from the previous close.
Is now the time to buy Marvell Technology? Access our full analysis report here, it's free.
Marvell Technology's shares are extremely volatile and have had 62 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today's move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.
The previous big move we wrote about was 4 days ago when the stock gained 2.7% on the news that weaker-than-expected U.S. employment data cooled Treasury yields, easing interest rate pressure. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that nonfarm payrolls increased by 29,000 in September, falling short of the 84,000 projected by economists polled by Dow Jones, while the unemployment rate rose to 4.2%.For the broader group, softer hiring eases interest-rate pressure on high-multiple growth equities by pulling borrowing costs lower.
However, further deceleration in the labor market risks dampening cyclical end-market demand across industrial and automotive chip channels.Semiconductor valuations expand when falling yields reduce the discount rate on long-duration earnings, provided enterprise infrastructure spending does not deteriorate.
Marvell Technology is up 214% since the beginning of the year, but at $280.82 per share, it is still trading 11.3% below its 52-week high of $316.43 from June 2026. Investors who bought $1,000 worth of Marvell Technology's shares 5 years ago would now be looking at an investment worth $4,405.

pages.text:
Marvell Technology Has Imploded Since June: One Defiant Wall Street Pro Says It’ll Double From Today
Marvell has shed a third of its value since summer even as its fundamentals keep accelerating, and one Wall Street analyst just planted a target so far above the current price that it reads like a provocation. Here is why…
Published September 15, 2026, 10:45am ET · 4 min read
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
A vibrant green arrow symbolizes the strong upward momentum of Hyperliquid (HYPE) as it pushes towards breaking its all-time price record. © Ja Crispy / Shutterstock.com
Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL | MRVL Price Prediction) currently trades at $218.82, well below the consensus 12-month analyst price target of $284.64. That gap implies roughly 30% upside to the average, but one outlier target from KeyBanc sits at $400, a call that would nearly double the stock and represents about 83% upside from here.
Marvell designs custom AI silicon and optical interconnect chips that hyperscalers stitch into their data center fabrics. The company’s data center segment now accounts for 79% of total revenue, up from 74% a year ago, which is why Wall Street tracks every hyperscaler order like a leading indicator.
The dislocation matters because Marvell’s fundamentals are still accelerating even as the stock has rolled over. Management just raised full-year guidance, expanded its Google partnership, and told investors custom silicon revenue will more than double in fiscal 2028. Yet the stock is down sharply from its summer high, setting up a classic gap between story and price.
What Actually Broke Marvell’s Summer Rally
The most immediate catalyst is today’s 7.32% single-session decline, part of a broad chip-sector selloff after prominent AI leaders publicly called for a slowdown in development pace, per a Wall Street Journal report on September 14. That reignited fears that hyperscaler capex could ease sooner than the bulls model.
Zoom out and the damage is worse. Marvell peaked at a 52-week high of $329.80 and now sits about 34% below that mark, a drawdown that qualifies as an implosion by any reasonable definition. The stock printed $255.88 the day it filed its Q2 fiscal 2027 results on August 27, meaning shares have lost meaningful ground even after a report that beat consensus.
The selloff is largely sector-wide rather than Marvell-specific. Broadcom is down 12.28% over the past month and NVIDIA is down 6.31%, so this reflects the AI cohort digesting a repricing of hyperscaler spending assumptions.
Analysts are staying put because the numbers keep going the other way. Marvell delivered record Q2 revenue of $2.739 billion, up 37% year-over-year, with data center revenue climbing 46%. Management raised the fiscal 2027 outlook to roughly $12 billion and now expects fiscal 2028 data center revenue to grow more than 60%.
Coverage skews decisively bullish. Alpha Vantage counts 8 Strong Buy, 31 Buy, 5 Hold, and 0 Sell ratings, and forward EPS estimates for fiscal 2028 have been revised upward 28 times in the trailing 30 days against just 1 downward revision. That signals a coverage universe leaning in.
KeyBanc’s $400 target rests on three pillars: custom AI ASIC wins with Amazon and Google, a near-monopoly position in 800G and 1.6T PAM4 DSPs and optical interconnects, and a data center revenue trajectory that KeyBanc models toward $18 billion by fiscal 2028. The October 6 Investor Day is the next catalyst analysts are circling to force a broader revaluation.
Where Marvell Stacks Up Against the Custom Silicon Cohort
The peer group sold off together over the past month, but the analyst-implied upside varies meaningfully across the cohort.
Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO) trades at $344.72, down 12.28% over the past month, against an average target of $531.85, implying roughly 54% upside. Ratings tilt heavily bullish at 8 Strong Buy, 37 Buy, and 4 Hold, and estimates keep drifting higher after another AI-fueled beat.
NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) sits at $210.96, off 6.31% in a month, versus a $327.18 average target and 55% upside. Coverage is nearly monolithic at 9 Strong Buy, 48 Buy, 2 Hold, and 1 Sell, though targets have not moved much since the Vera Rubin ramp was already priced in.
Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) trades at $493.41, up 130.39% year to date, against a $615.07 target that implies just 25% upside. Analysts are constructive with 4 Strong Buy, 39 Buy, and 11 Hold, but the easy re-rating is behind AMD after the OpenAI and Meta deployment deals.
The largest analyst-implied upside in this group sits at NVIDIA and Broadcom on the consensus reading, but KeyBanc’s Marvell call at $400 dwarfs every peer target on a percentage basis. That is what makes Marvell the asymmetric name in the cohort if the bull thesis holds.
What the Setup Looks Like in Hard Numbers
Marvell is up 157.87% year to date and 225.6% over the past year, while the S&P 500 has returned 11.57% and 15.73% over the same windows. The rally has cooled recently, with the stock essentially flat since June 1 at -0.25%.
The valuation reflects that run. Marvell trades at a trailing PE of 78 and a forward PE of 56, with a market cap near $212 billion. Analyst targets are one data point among many, and the 44 analysts covering the stock have a wide range around the KeyBanc call.
Marvell looks compelling here if the custom silicon ramp lands as guided and the October Investor Day gives the Street a credible bridge to KeyBanc’s fiscal 2028 revenue math. The path back to the $284 consensus runs through one more raise, sustained data center growth above 60%, and a scale-up optics narrative that management is clearly setting up. But the setup weakens if hyperscaler capex assumptions get repriced lower, or if customer concentration risk turns concrete through a big Amazon or Google decision to move more silicon in-house.
My lean is cautiously constructive. The consensus 30% upside looks reasonable given accelerating fundamentals, and the KeyBanc case, while stretched, is not fanciful given design win momentum (we reverse-engineered what the biggest AI chip winners looked like early in a free playbook you can grab here). This is a name where the October Investor Day matters more than the daily price action, and the event looks more consequential than any single session ahead of it.

AI Stocks are responding to changing sector and macro signals.
AI momentum, oil prices and bond yields are shaping market attention.
Marvell Technology Group Ltd (NASDAQ:MRVL)
, a constituent of the Nasdaq Composite and the [Nasdaq-100], is in focus among AI Stocks today. Marvell Technology is a semiconductor company focused on data infrastructure, custom AI silicon and high-speed connectivity. The stock is drawing attention as Wall Street weighs AI momentum, shifting oil prices and bond yields, with investors looking closely at how individual companies are positioned for a more selective market.
US equities are trading against a backdrop of shifting signals. The AI rally that has supported technology stocks has shown signs of losing momentum at times, while oil prices have swung with developments in the Middle East and changing supply expectations. Treasury yields remain a key reference point for valuations, especially for rate-sensitive sectors. In this environment, sector rotation has become more pronounced, with investors moving between growth, defensive and cyclical stocks depending on the latest economic and policy news.
Marvell Technology designs semiconductors that move, store and process data across data centers, carrier networks, enterprise systems and automotive platforms. In recent years the company has leaned heavily into data-center demand, where it supplies electro-optics products such as DSPs used in high-speed optical links, along with custom application-specific chips built in partnership with large cloud operators. That custom silicon business has made Marvell one of the more closely watched names in the AI supply chain, since hyperscalers increasingly design their own accelerators to complement merchant GPUs. The company has also narrowed its focus over time, stepping back from some non-core areas to concentrate resources on the fastest-growing infrastructure markets.
The stock often trades as a read-through on hyperscaler capital spending. When AI enthusiasm strengthens, investors tend to focus on Marvell's optical and custom programmes; when the market questions the durability of AI budgets, the stock can be sensitive to shifts in sentiment. The competitive landscape includes Broadcom in custom accelerators and a range of players in optical connectivity, which keeps design wins and customer concentration under close review.
The AI group has become one of the main drivers of US equity performance, but leadership within it has narrowed. Chipmakers, networking suppliers, server builders and data platforms all depend on the same wave of hyperscaler capital spending, so a single comment from a major cloud operator can move the whole group. Recent sessions have shown that enthusiasm can fade quickly when investors question valuations or the timing of returns on AI investment. That makes company-level evidence, such as order backlogs, customer wins and margin trends, more important than broad theme exposure. Power availability and export controls on advanced chips have also become important constraints on how fast AI infrastructure can be deployed.
Within AI stocks, investors typically separate companies by where they sit in the value chain. Chip designers and equipment suppliers are most directly exposed to data-center build-outs, networking and server companies benefit as clusters scale, and software and data platforms depend on enterprises turning AI experiments into production workloads. Key signals include hyperscaler capital expenditure guidance, order backlogs, gross margins and customer concentration. Because expectations are high across the group, even solid results can lead to share-price declines if guidance falls short of what the market has priced in.
The market's reading of Marvell Technology also depends on macro conditions. Bond yields influence how investors discount future cash flows and how much financing costs, while oil prices affect inflation expectations and spending patterns. Geopolitical developments can move commodity markets and shift risk appetite quickly. At the same time, the strength of AI-related spending continues to set the tone for large parts of the equity market, influencing sector rotation from one session to the next.
Key items to track include updates on custom silicon programmes, demand for 800G and next-generation optical products, data-center revenue mix, and commentary on recovery in enterprise networking, carrier and automotive markets.
As with any listed company, Marvell Technology faces risks that could affect its performance. These include changes in demand for its products or services, competitive pressure, regulatory and policy developments, and shifts in the broader economic environment. Execution on strategic priorities and the ability to manage costs in an uncertain market will also influence results. Readers following the stock should weigh both the opportunities and the challenges described above.
How Marvell Technology fits the AI Stocks theme
Within AI Stocks, Marvell Technology offers a useful example of how company-specific factors interact with sector-wide trends. When the group moves together, broad themes such as interest rates or commodity prices are usually the driver. When Marvell Technology diverges from peers, the explanation is more likely to be found in its own operating results, strategic decisions or news flow. Watching how the stock behaves relative to its sector can therefore provide insight into how the market views its individual prospects.
Investor sentiment toward Marvell Technology can change quickly as new information emerges. Earnings reports, management commentary, analyst updates and industry news all play a role. In the current environment, where sector leadership is narrow and macro signals are mixed, the market has tended to reward companies that show clear evidence of demand and disciplined execution, while punishing those that disappoint on growth or margins.
Marvell Technology remains a relevant name to watch in AI Stocks as the market weighs AI momentum, oil prices and interest rates. Its business fundamentals, sector conditions and macro backdrop together explain the current attention. Readers can use upcoming company updates and industry data to judge how the story develops.

The chipmaker also raised its fiscal 2028 revenue goal to $20 billion, well above the analyst consensus of $18.2 billion
By Colleen Cabili·2 min read·Updated October 6, 2026
Marvell Technology held its investor day on Tuesday, setting a fiscal 2031 revenue target of $70 billion to $90 billion and lifting its fiscal 2028 goal to $20 billion. Marvell stock rose roughly 4% on the day.
The fiscal 2031 range marks Marvell's first-ever guidance for that year. The midpoint sits far above the analyst consensus of $47 billion, according to CNBC. The bottom of the range alone is more than 50% above the $45 billion that Piper Sandler had modeled for fiscal 2031, according to Benzinga. For context, Marvell posted $8.2 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.
The new fiscal 2028 target of $20 billion represents an increase from the $18 billion figure Marvell had provided when it reported second-quarter earnings in late August. Marvell attributed the additional $2 billion to demand for data center connectivity products, including interconnect scale-up optics and switching, the company said. Fiscal 2027 revenue is still expected at around $12 billion, the company said.
Marvell's business serving AI data centers breaks into two main areas. The company helps large cloud customers — including Amazon $AMZN and Alphabet $GOOGL — design and manufacture custom AI chips. It also makes the optical and networking chips that move data within and across data center racks. Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy said Marvell's AI addressable market could reach $400 billion by 2030, according to Benzinga.
Supporting the long-term outlook, Marvell forecast that capital expenditures for data centers would hit $3 trillion by 2030, compounding at roughly 35% annually between 2025 and 2030, the company said. Marvell noted that its projections account for spending growth slowing from its current pace as the forecast period progresses, the company said.
Marvell's custom chip business has a major customer in Google, with whom it expanded a commercial agreement in late July covering custom processors and related chips. Murphy indicated that the financial contribution from that agreement is not expected to materialize in a meaningful way until fiscal 2029 at the earliest, the company said.
Taken together, the successive upward revisions amount to a roughly 54% increase in the fiscal 2028 target over the span of about 10 months, according to Benzinga. Marvell stock has gained 217% over the past 12 months. Shares of data center connectivity peers Astera Labs and Credo Technology also rose Tuesday, gaining 8% and 6%, respectively, according to Benzinga.

Marvell Technology (MRVL +5.81%) finally put a number on its long-term goals. Talking to investors in New York on Tuesday, management said Marvell sees revenue of around $20 billion in fiscal 2028 and $70 billion to $90 billion in fiscal 2031 (the year ending in early 2031).
For context, Marvell took in $8.2 billion of revenue in fiscal 2026, the year that ended in January. So the latest range is about 8.5 to 11 times last fiscal year's sales. Management also pegged the size of the market it's chasing at about $400 billion by 2030.
Shares jumped after the event and were around $290 as of this writing. At that price, the stock trades at about 43 times the earnings expected for fiscal 2028, so it's not cheap on near-term numbers.
Compared with the company's own long-term targets, though, I think the price looks much more reasonable.
Image source: Getty Images.
Marvell's fiscal 2028 revenue forecast has risen in each of its past two updates. In May, management called for around $16.5 billion. In August, it upped that to around $18 billion, on top of about $12 billion expected for fiscal 2027. Now it sees about $20 billion, an 11% gain over about six weeks.
The growth Marvell expects for that year has climbed with it, from around 45% in May to about 50% in August. If fiscal 2027 lands near that $12 billion forecast, $20 billion would mean growth of about 67%. In other words, Marvell keeps finding more growth for the same year, even as the company gets bigger.
Reported results are going the same way. Revenue rose 37% year over year in the fiscal second quarter (the period ended Aug. 1), up from 28% the quarter before, and the company forecast more than 50% growth this quarter.
The fiscal 2031 range calls for more of the same. Going from $20 billion to $70 billion to $90 billion in three years would take annual growth of around 52% to 65% -- about the rate Marvell now expects for fiscal 2028, held for another three years.
Today's price looks modest against the targets
On the August earnings call, Dan Durn, Marvell's chief financial officer, said its non-GAAP (adjusted) operating margin would probably hit the company's 38% to 40% long-term target range by the fiscal fourth quarter and reach the top end in fiscal 2028. He added Marvell would reset that long-term model at the investor day. The adjusted operating margin was 36.6% last quarter, up from 34.8% a year before.
Even at the old 38% to 40% range, $70 billion to $90 billion of revenue would mean around $27 billion to $36 billion of adjusted operating profit in fiscal 2031. Marvell's market value, meanwhile, is about $255 billion. So the stock sells for around 7 to 10 times the fiscal 2031 operating profit implied by its own targets.
Operating profit isn't earnings, of course. But with Marvell expecting an adjusted tax rate of only about 13% in fiscal 2028, taxes might not change the picture much.
If Marvell hit only half the low end of its range, or $35 billion, a 38% margin would mean shares cost about 19 times operating profit. For a company growing so fast, I'd call that a fair price for a disappointing outcome.
How solid is the range?
Of course, a target isn't a contract. And the $20 billion gap between the low and high ends of the fiscal 2031 range matches Marvell's entire fiscal 2028 target.
I couldn't find any disclosed customer commitments backing the range. CEO Matt Murphy said custom chip programs with cloud giants such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon could lift revenue as they grow after 2029.
Even the custom deal Marvell has detailed most fully leaves the buying up to the customer. A warrant Marvell issued in August to Google, a unit of Alphabet, vests as Google buys custom products, up to $120 billion worth through fiscal 2033. But the filing describing it calls the purchases "discretionary."

Growth in custom chips also drags on profitability. Management said the custom ramp is why its adjusted gross margin guidance for the fiscal third quarter is 57.5% to 58.5%, below 58.9% last quarter.
And spending on artificial intelligence could slow long before 2031.
Still, I don't think Marvell needs to hit its range for the stock to do well from here. At about $290, shares look fairly priced even against half the low end, and the shorter-term outlook keeps rising. I think the stock is worth buying today, even after Tuesday's jump. But I'd expect big swings in the share price ahead.

Two of Wall Street's better-known research shops moved in tandem on Tuesday, lifting their price objectives on Marvell Technology after the chipmaker sketched out a far more ambitious revenue map at its investor day. Jefferies raised its target to $450 from $325 while keeping a Buy rating, and Evercore ISI lifted its own to $433 from $275 with an Outperform stance intact.
The stock caught a modest bid in premarket trading, adding 0.7% to change hands at EUR 256.85. That follows a 5.6% surge in the prior session that carried the shares to a close of EUR 255.15, a move attributed chiefly to the upgraded long-range forecasts and helped along by a broadly firmer technology tape.
A Bigger Pie by 2028 — and a Far Bigger One by 2031
At the center of the analysts' enthusiasm sits Marvell's revised outlook. Management now targets roughly $20 billion in revenue for fiscal 2028, up from the $18 billion goal it had set out only in August. The company also raised its revenue objective for custom solutions in fiscal 2029 to more than $12 billion.
The horizon stretches much further, though. For fiscal 2031, Marvell laid out a revenue range of $70 billion to $90 billion alongside adjusted earnings per share — non-GAAP — of $30 or more. Management anchored those figures to the breakneck expansion of the artificial intelligence market, which Marvell sizes at roughly $400 billion in total addressable demand for AI applications by 2030.
Jefferies leaned explicitly on that fiscal 2031 framework, pointing to the connectivity segment's potential as the justification for its richer valuation. Evercore's revision followed the same logic, with both houses rewarding the company's long-term positioning rather than near-term results.
Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying Marvell Technology?
Substrates, a Dividend, and a Routine Insider Sale
Capacity is the quiet prerequisite for all of that growth, and Marvell is moving to secure it. AT&S announced on September 22 an expanded collaboration with the chipmaker aimed at scaling output of advanced IC substrates — the building blocks required for next-generation AI and cloud infrastructure.
On the capital-returns side, the board declared a regular quarterly dividend of $0.06 per share on September 25. Shareholders of record as of October 9, 2026 will receive the payout on October 29, 2026.
A filing also disclosed that a family trust tied to President and COO Chris Koopmans sold 10,000 shares on October 1 under a pre-arranged Rule 10b5-1 trading plan. The manager retains indirect ownership of 207,941 shares following the transaction.
The rally has narrowed the gap to the 52-week high of EUR 290.35, leaving the stock about 12% below that peak. Since the start of the year, the shares have climbed 250%.
That kind of run leaves little room for error. Celebrating targets set years into the future effectively prices in a largely frictionless execution, and any unexpected slowdown in hyperscaler infrastructure budgets would land hard on a valuation this rich. The distance to those out-year goals is considerable, and a business that must multiply several times over by the start of the next decade offers no cushion for operational disappointment.
Even so, the strategic case remains intact. Marvell's grip on custom silicon for data centers has become central to the AI supply chain, and the steady dividend alongside heavy investment in future chip generations signals both discipline and confidence. For now, the balance of opportunity still tilts toward the specialized data-center chip story — provided the company delivers on the very promises that sent its shares flying.

Several key AI infrastructure companies, including CoreWeave (CRWV), Dell Technologies (DELL), Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE), and Broadcom (AVGO), have also raised their revenue expectations in recent months, indicating that the AI infrastructure buildout is far from over.

The common thread is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Companies across the infrastructure stack are starting to see stronger demand translate into more visibility for revenue several years out.
From custom AI chips and networking equipment to AI-optimized servers and the data centers needed to house them, the spending cycle is broadening across the ecosystem.
MRVL stock jumped nearly 6% Tuesday following its outlook at its Investor Day event, although shares fell slightly in premarket trading Wednesday.

Marvell laid out a fiscal 2031 revenue target of $70 billion-$90 billion, implying a massive expansion from the $8.2 billion it generated in fiscal 2026, which ended in January 2026.
Marvell expects its custom-made AI chips business to generate about $30 billion in revenue by fiscal 2031. Beyond that, the company sees more opportunities in other data-center components, including networking chips and technology that helps AI systems process data faster.
The company also raised its fiscal 2028 revenue target to approximately $20 billion, from $18 billion previously, and expects more than $12 billion of custom revenue in fiscal 2029.

Importantly, this was not a sudden change in tone. In Q2, Marvell reported record revenue of $2.74 billion, up 37% year over year, while data-center revenue surged 46%. CEO Matt Murphy said at the time that AI-related bookings remained “exceptionally robust” and that growth should accelerate through the rest of fiscal 2027.
Analysts React To Marvell’s Lofty Outlook
Jefferies raised its price target on MRVL to $450 from $325, saying Marvell’s FY31 outlook puts “connectivity at the center of the story,” with interconnect potentially reaching $37.5 billion and custom revenue approaching $30 billion.
Evercore ISI lifted its target to $433 from $275, highlighting Marvell’s IP portfolio and flexible business model across merchant, semi-custom and custom solutions.

Raymond James similarly called the FY31 outlook “extraordinary,” saying scale-up connectivity and optics could prove “at least as important” to the long-term story as custom compute.
Morningstar raised its fair value estimate to $360 from $300, citing a roughly 40% increase in its fiscal 2031 revenue and EPS estimates. It acknowledged valuation concerns after the stock’s sharp run-up, but said the company’s expected growth makes the premium easier to justify.

Marvell Technology (MRVL) Stock: Gains as AI Chip Demand Fuels Bullish Forecast
Marvell raises its FY2028 revenue target as custom silicon and data center demand strengthen growth
By Yasmin WernerOctober 6, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Marvell stock gains as FY2028 revenue guidance rises to $20 billion
The company expects fiscal 2028 revenue growth of about 67% year over year
AI chip and data center demand remain central to Marvell’s growth outlook
Amazon, Google, and Microsoft support Marvell’s custom silicon expansion
Marvell shares have climbed more than 240% since the start of the year
Marvell Technology (MRVL) stock gained 5.64% to $286.58 during Tuesday trading after the company raised its long-term revenue guidance. The semiconductor company now expects fiscal 2028 revenue to reach about $20 billion. The stronger forecast reflects expanding demand for custom chips and data center infrastructure.
The updated outlook marks a significant increase from Marvell’s previous fiscal 2028 revenue target. Management had projected about $18 billion in August, while market estimates had centered near $18.2 billion. Therefore, the latest guidance places Marvell above its earlier expectations for the period.
Marvell also expects fiscal 2028 revenue to rise about 67% from the previous year. Chief Executive Matt Murphy presented the updated targets during the company’s investor day conference Tuesday. The announcement strengthened attention around Marvell’s growing exposure to large-scale computing infrastructure.
Marvell Raises Fiscal 2028 Revenue Target
Marvell expects demand from large technology companies to support its revenue expansion through fiscal 2028. The company develops custom silicon and networking products for high-performance computing systems. These products help data centers move information efficiently between processors, memory, and other infrastructure components.
The company estimates its total addressable market related to artificial intelligence could reach approximately $400 billion by 2030. Marvell works on custom silicon programs with major technology companies, including Amazon, Google, and Microsoft. Consequently, these partnerships give Marvell exposure to continued spending on large data center projects.
Marvell competes directly with Broadcom across several semiconductor infrastructure markets. Both companies provide networking technologies and custom processors used in advanced computing systems. However, Marvell has expanded its position through custom chip programs and high-speed connectivity products.
Semiconductor Demand Supports Marvell Growth
Semiconductor companies have benefited from rising spending on computing capacity and large data centers this year. Marvell has participated in that expansion through products designed for networking and custom processing workloads. Meanwhile, technology companies continue building infrastructure that requires faster data transfer and greater computing efficiency.
Marvell also gained broader market exposure after joining the S&P 500 index in June. The inclusion followed substantial share appreciation during 2026 and increased the company’s presence within major equity benchmarks. Marvell shares have climbed more than 240% since the beginning of the year.
Earlier this year, Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang highlighted Marvell’s position within the semiconductor industry. The company has since continued expanding its custom silicon and networking businesses. Its latest fiscal 2028 forecast now reinforces management’s expectations for substantial revenue growth.
Marvell Expands Role in Data Center Infrastructure
Marvell designs high-speed infrastructure that connects processors across modern data centers. Its portfolio includes networking, connectivity, storage, and custom semiconductor products. These technologies support cloud computing providers that require large amounts of processing capacity.
The company has increasingly focused on custom silicon programs for major hyperscale customers. Those projects allow large technology companies to develop specialized chips for specific computing workloads. Marvell provides design expertise and semiconductor technologies that support those customized platforms.
The revised revenue outlook adds another growth target to Marvell’s expanding data center business. Management now expects stronger fiscal 2028 sales than projected only two months earlier. The increase reflects the company’s larger role in custom silicon and high-speed data center infrastructure.

The company drew attention after demonstrating advanced optical interconnect technology designed to move data faster between the components of artificial intelligence systems. The showcase, tied to a leading optical communications conference, highlighted Marvell Technology's push into the plumbing that links accelerators, switches, and memory across sprawling data centers. Shares advanced as the market digested the announcement, placing the name among the more active constituents of the Nasdaq Composite during a strong stretch for infrastructure chips.
The showcase resonated because connectivity has emerged as one of the defining challenges of large-scale computing. As clusters grow, the difficulty of moving data quickly between components has become a genuine constraint on performance. Marvell Technology's demonstrations spoke directly to this pain point, offering technology aimed at relieving the bottleneck. The market's swift reaction reflected recognition that advances in connectivity can unlock the full value of the accelerators operators have been racing to deploy across their facilities.

Its portfolio spans custom silicon built for specific customers, high-speed connectivity chips, optical technology, and networking components. The firm has carved out a role as a supplier of the specialized parts that stitch together large computing systems. As artificial intelligence workloads have grown, the demand for faster, more efficient data movement has placed Marvell Technology's products at the center of the infrastructure conversation.
The company's breadth across custom silicon, connectivity, and optical technology gives it multiple points of contact with the systems powering advanced computing. Rather than betting on a single product line, it supplies a range of components that operators need to assemble and scale their clusters. This diversity lets the firm participate in the buildout from several angles, cushioning it against shifts in any one segment. Its role as a supplier of the connective and custom elements of large systems has grown steadily more central.
The bottleneck in modern computing clusters increasingly lies not in raw processing but in moving data between components fast enough to keep accelerators fed. Marvell Technology's optical interconnect demonstrations addressed exactly this challenge, showcasing technology that pushes more data through each connection. Advanced optical modules and co-packaged optics aim to scale the connectivity of large systems, allowing operators to link more accelerators without choking on data transfer limits. This focus on the connective tissue of data centers has become a defining part of the company's story.
Co-packaged optics and advanced optical modules represent a frontier in how data centers scale, capable of moving far more information through each connection while managing power. As clusters expand, the limits of conventional connectivity become more apparent, elevating the value of optical approaches. Marvell Technology's demonstrations positioned it at this frontier, showcasing technology designed to keep pace with the escalating demands of advanced computing. This focus on the connective tissue of systems has become a signature element of its story.
